title: A direction that does not turn

text.guided:
Most vectors are **turned** by a matrix. But some special directions are only stretched: the vector comes out on the same line it went in on. Those are the **eigenvectors**.

If the matrix stretches x by 2 and keeps y, then a vector along the x axis just gets twice as long: it keeps its direction.
text.fast: An eigenvector satisfies $M\,v = \lambda\,v$: same direction, scaled by the eigenvalue $\lambda$.

examples.games: Pulling a stretchy toy along its length keeps it straight; pulling it sideways bends it.
examples.physics: The principal axes of a deformation are the directions that are stretched without being rotated.
examples.sport: A ball kicked straight along the wind only goes faster or slower; kicked across it, it curves.

robot: Most beams get bent by the lens. A few special directions come out straight.

mission.games: Aim the laser so the lens does not bend it.
mission.physics: Find a direction the lens only stretches, never turns.
mission.sport: Kick along the wind and the ball flies straight. Find that line.

title: How much it stretches

text.guided:
When a vector keeps its direction, it can still change **length**. The number that says by how much is the **eigenvalue**: M·v = λ·v. A negative eigenvalue flips the vector to the other side but keeps it on the same line.

For [[2, 0], [0, 3]], a vector along x is stretched by 2 and a vector along y by 3.
text.fast: $M v = \lambda v$. $\lambda$ is read off as the factor along the eigen-direction.

examples.games: A zoom that doubles width and triples height: along each axis, the zoom factor is the eigenvalue.
examples.physics: The eigenvalue along a principal axis is the stretch ratio in that direction.
examples.sport: A pitch stretched 2× in length and 3× in width: along each line, the stretch factor is the eigenvalue.

robot: Along a straight direction, the lens only stretches. The stretch factor is the eigenvalue.

check.prompt: The matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]] is read as î → (2, 0) and ĵ → (0, 3). By what factor is a vector along the x axis stretched?

title: Sometimes there is none

text.guided:
A quarter turn sends î to (0, 1) and ĵ to (−1, 0): **every** direction is rotated, so no vector stays on its own line. Some matrices have no real eigenvectors at all.

When you see a pure turn, do not hunt for a direction: say there is no straight path.
text.fast: A rotation by an angle that is not 0° or 180° has no real eigenvector: its eigenvalues are complex.

examples.games: A camera that spins the whole scene leaves no object pointing the same way.
examples.physics: A pure rotation of the plane keeps no direction fixed.
examples.sport: Spin the whole pitch around the centre spot: no player keeps facing the same direction.

robot: A pure rotation turns every beam. Sometimes the right answer is: no straight path.

mission.games: This lens spins everything. Is there any straight path?
mission.physics: A quarter-turn lens. Does any beam keep its direction?
mission.sport: The whole pitch spins. Does any player keep facing the same way?
